item.title: Kyle Hamilton: Think we have a great plan to keep Brazil travel from hindering us
item.description: There was a lot of focus on travel plans leading into the Week 1 game between the 49ers and Rams in Australia, but there's been less attention paid to the Ravens and Cowboys as they prepare to play in Rio this week.
item.content:encoded:
There was a lot of focus on travel plans leading into the Week 1 game between the 49ers and Rams in Australia, but there's been less attention paid to the Ravens and Cowboys as they prepare to play in Rio this week.

There's good reason for that as it is a much less severe time difference for both teams, but there's still an overnight flight for both teams on Thursday night and that will be different than other games that take place in different time zones. On Wednesday, Ravens safety Kyle Hamilton said that he thinks the team has a good handle on how to approach Sunday's game.

"I think the staff — credit to everybody involved — has a great plan in place for us when we get down there, and [we are] going to try to take advantage of the travel in a way that it is not hindering us coming into Sunday," Hamilton said, via the team's website. "I think the words 'flying out of our skin' were used in the team meeting, so that is the ultimate goal. Obviously, both sides are dealing with it, so there are really no excuses to be made but, I think we have a good plan in place and good organization when we get down there."

The interest in the travel plans for the Australia game was piqued by the different approaches that the two teams took to the trip. With the Cowboys and Ravens following the same schedule, it's unlikely to be much of a talking point after the game either.

item.title: Why Lions WR Isaac TeSlaa has limited targets, and when that will change
item.description: Detroit Lions WR Isaac TeSlaa has been getting limited targets, but Scottie Montgomery explained how that will change.
item.content:encoded:
Through two games, Detroit Lions receiver Isaac TeSlaa has just six targets and two catches—one being a garbage time conversion on fourth-and-18 while down 17 points with about two minutes left. Given how much draft capital the Lions have spent on the second-year receiver, some fans have expressed frustration with his lack of production.

On Wednesday, Lions associate head coach and wide receivers coach Scottie Montgomery addressed TeSlaa’s lack of production so far. The main reasoning for it has little to do with TeSlaa himself and more to do with the fact that the Lions are just extremely deep when it comes to weapons in the passing game. TeSlaa is essentially fifth in line behind Amon-Ra St. Brown, Jameson Williams, Sam LaPorta, and Jahmyr Gibbs.

“Tes [TeSlaa], his opportunities are going to be limited just because of how we’re built as an offense, whether it be at tight end or it be at wideout, whether it be in the backfield, who we have a phenomenal player in the backfield,” Montgomery said. “So what he’s going to have to do is—all of his (opportunities) are going to be critical. They’re going to be fourth down, they’re going to be red zone, they’re going to be third downs.”

Montgomery said teams have played Detroit’s offense a little differently than in previous years. The Lions are used to defenses shading coverages toward St. Brown, but the All-Pro receiver has surprisingly been put in a lot of one-on-one situations. There’s been very little need for Jared Goff to go beyond his first or second progressions thus far. But Montgomery expects that to eventually change—especially this week against the Jets and Aaron Glenn, who knows how dangerous St. Brown can be. That is when TeSlaa is going to have to show up.

“We have to judge [TeSlaa] off of those plays until we get everything rolling to a point to where we are equally distributing because of the coverage and how they’re moving to Saint,” Montgomery said. “But at this point in time right now, it’s been really one of those situations where a lot of times our first in progression has been open, our second in progression has been open, and sometimes when you’re not first or second in the progression, you have to wait until you get going.”

In the meantime, TeSlaa has been doing everything right away from the play. That involves doing the dirty work of blocking, being physical, and sometimes being so tight to the line that he’s essentially playing as another tight end.

“Right now, he’s playing harder than damn-near anybody that we have on our offensive side of the ball,” Montgomery said. “He is mixing it up, he’s physical. And that’s what you have to do when you’re in that role. A lot of guys have never played in that role.”

Montgomery believes as TeSlaa continues to gain this reputation as a dirty-work player that is an asset in the run game, they will be able to build plays off those tendencies. That’s when TeSlaa could become a serious weapon in a room full of weapons.

“When you look at that, those situations the dirty work, all of those plays that no one else wants to make—and now because of that, we’re able to use those tendencies and create a bigger play for him in the game because some of the dirty work that he has,” Montgomery said. “And then all of a sudden, it’s that, ‘We’ve got to get him the ball more.’ So we look forward to those things happening.”

TeSlaa was taken the the third round of the 2025 NFL Draft after Detroit traded two 2026 third-round picks to come up and get him. In his career, he has 18 catches for 265 yards and six touchdowns, although much of his production came after LaPorta went down with an injury last year. The production may not be there, but Montgomery believes they are still getting plenty of value out of him.

“For what he’s able to do for us, he’s able to stretch the field, he can block in the box—those two deals don’t usually work together Outside receivers usually don’t have the ability to block (in) the box,” Montgomery said. “He gives us the ability now to take some of those shots off of Saint, use Saint in different situations. He can also clear down the middle of the field. He has short-area quickness in some of those tight spots where he’s a big body, he can make plays. We’ll start to see more of it as we go forward, but he has a tremendous value on this team.”

item.title: Mike Macdonald apologizes to Sean Payton for past story on cheating dispute
item.description: Seahawks coach Mike Macdonald apologized for remarks about a past dispute with Broncos coach Sean Payton, calling it a “lesson learned.”
item.content:encoded:
Seattle Seahawks head coach Mike Macdonald has publicly apologized for remarks he made regarding a past dispute with Denver Broncos coach Sean Payton, describing the episode as a "lesson learned."

Macdonald addressed the situation during an appearance on “In Depth With Graham Bensinger,” referencing a 2024 dispute with Payton. He explained that his comments were never intended for public consumption, but they quickly gained traction on the social media platform X.

The dispute centered on Payton’s 2024 accusation that the Seahawks had cheated while preparing for the season opener against the Broncos. According to Macdonald, Denver mistakenly believed that Seattle had sent someone to the Broncos’ training camp to secretly film and relay plays. In reality, Macdonald clarified, the Seahawks’ coaching staff gained insights from footage posted by fans who attended the Broncos’ open practices and shared plays publicly on the social media platform X.

Payton confirmed that Macdonald reached out early in the week to apologize.

Payton assured him there were no hard feelings, emphasizing that he understood how speaking about past events can sometimes lead to misunderstandings. He reiterated his respect for Macdonald, stating he had "a ton of respect" for the Seahawks coach.

"I've got to be better in that moment (in) understanding, look, I'm responsible for what I say really no matter the circumstance, whether you're miked up, whether you're not, whether you have a certain understanding," Macdonald said when speaking to reporters. "So, I fell short in that moment. It stings for me, frankly, but it's something I'm definitely going to learn from, and it's just a good example of (how) we've got to take responsibility for the things that we say."

More: Mike Macdonald explains how Seahawks used social media to scout Broncos in 2024

Although the incident brought up past tensions, Macdonald emphasized that he and Payton are on good terms after their conversation and that both are ready to move forward.

"I'll say, I have a great deal of respect for him and his program," Macdonald said. "He's a phenomenal football coach. It’s been great getting to know him at the owners’ meetings over the past couple of years. He’s been awesome."

This article originally appeared on USA TODAY: Mike Macdonald apologizes to Sean Payton for past story on cheating dispute

item.title: Value of Things: By the Numbers
item.description: How will the Colts and Texans attack each other on Sunday?
item.content:encoded:
Sunday sees a matchup of two 0-2 football teams that have lost to two playoff bound teams in their first two weeks. In other words, neither fan base knows for sure whether the lack of success is a factor of difficult opponents or glaring roster holes. Obviously, it is likely it will be a combination. So, the numbers we look at may not actually be indicative of the quality of the unit. That is a part of the peril of handicapping early season matchups,

The Texans in particular showed glaring defensive holes in week one and glaring offensive holes in week two. It is almost a version of Dr. Heckyl and Mr. Jackass. The Colts have some of the same issues going on on both sides of the ball. It will be a battle to see who the real team is. One will walk away feeling some hope for the rest of the season. The other will be entering desperation mode. Of course, the Texans have been there on more than one occasion. Maybe they work best in desperation mode.

The Numbers

I should point out that the Texans have a major identity crisis on their hands. They say they are a hard-nosed physical running team. Their numbers say they are a passing team. That’s a significant issue we will have to sink our teeth into as the season goes if those trends continue. Obviously, a part of that comes from playing from behind for much of the first two games. Numbers always have a context.

The Colts numbers also have a context. The Chiefs and Ravens are two of the better offenses in the AFC, so either the Colts are bad or they just look bad. This Sunday will tell the tale on both accounts. So, let’s take a look at what each team will try to do to each other.

What will the Colts offense do?

Jonathan “Zachary” Taylor is one of the best five backs in football year in a year out. He doesn’t get the press that those other guys get primarily because he doesn’t show up in prime time nearly as much as those other backs. Plus, to call Daniel Jones a part of the middle class of quarterbacks is doing a whole lot of heavy lifting. Jones can be effective with his feet and when used in concert with Taylor gives the Colts one of the most dynamic rushing attacks in the NFL. Jones is facing the same issue this week that Stroud faced last week. He will not have Alex Pierce, so there will be limited targets. Ty Warren is a weapon to be sure and one to watch in the play action game and on run pass options. The Colts will be successful if they can stay ahead of the chains. If not, it could be a long day for Jones.

What will the Colts defense do to the Texans?

The Texans do not have a back the caliber of Derrick Henry or Kenneth Walker. David Montgomery has spent most of his career as a complimentary back. He has been one of the better ones, but he is not capable of carrying a team on his own. This is particularly true if that team struggles up front. So, if you shut down Montgomery and Woody Marks like the Bengals did and the Texans offense starts to look really ordinary really fast. Of course, they have also struggled against the pass, but Stroud is not Lamar Jackson or Patrick Mahomes. So, there is some hope on their end.

What will the Texans offense do to the Colts?

Here we go again. There is what they want to do and what they actually can do. The best thing a football team can do is lean into what they do well. Right now, the Texans have been effectively passing the football. At press time, Nico Collins’ status is still unknown. He has torched the Colts in the past, so we could probably start there if he is able to play. If he isn’t then Nick Caley will need to be creative. It might start by admitting that what is left over is not what we would call traditional playmakers. Again, the best teams are the teams that acknowledge what is and then lean into what is. We can hope for a hard-nosed rushing attack that takes pressure off of Stroud. Hope might be all we have at this point. One thing is for sure, if you can’t run on the Colts then you probably can’t run on anyone.

What will the Texans defense do to the Colts?

Like with the Colts, the Texans pass defense looks bad, but anyone can look bad against Josh Allen and Joe Burrow. What you are is made up of who you are in a majority of your data points. That is done over the course of 17 weeks and the playoffs. If Daniel Jones torches them then we know we have a problem. So, the key is slowing down Taylor. That will be easier said than done because he is likely the best back they have faced to this point in the season. If they can keep the Colts behind the sticks then they win the game. Period.

item.title: NFL Week 3 Survivor/Eliminator Picks
item.description: With 1:56 left Sunday, the Eagles were down 20-17 and looked like they might lose to the Titans. With 10 seconds left, they were still down. They scored a touchdown then, and even if they hadn’t they were close enough…
item.content:encoded:
With 1:56 left Sunday, the Eagles were down 20-17 and looked like they might lose to the Titans. With 10 seconds left, they were still down. They scored a touchdown then, and even if they hadn’t they were close enough that they were likely to kick a field goal and send it to overtime, but still, my Week 2 NFL Survivor (or NFL Eliminator, if that’s your jam) pick was that close to missing. Coming off a Week 1 miss (stupid Chargers), sure, I was more than a little scared that I’d fall to 0-2 and look like a big ol’ dummy. As it is, I’m only a half dummy. Below, check out my Week 3 pick for Survivor contests. And while we’re here, you can use our NFL Betting Model and our Bet Tracker to make a pick for yourself.

NFL Survivor Picks for Week 3

Every week, we have the same process. We eliminate teams in groups until we narrow it down to our real considerations. Start with all 32, whittle it down. And remember — this game is “once you use a team, they’re off the board,” so it’s not always just a matter of taking the team you think will win. There has to be some strategy. I can’t pick a team I’ve picked before, but you might not have tailed me, so previously used teams are eligible until the end.

Opponent Is Too Good

Maybe these are good teams, maybe not, but it’s too hard to trust them given who they are facing. This is a 10-team list every week (fewer when there are byes); we are eliminating anyone facing a top-10 team in our FTN NFL Power Rankings. Arizona Cardinals (@ San Francisco) Dallas Cowboys (vs. Baltimore) Denver Broncos (vs. LA Rams) Jacksonville Jaguars (vs. New England) Los Angeles Chargers (@ Buffalo) Los Angeles Rams (@ Denver) Miami Dolphins (vs. Kansas City) New England Patriots (@ Jacksonville) Pittsburgh Steelers (vs. Cincinnati) Washington Commanders (vs. Seattle) Some of these teams will win but you can’t confidently say so, considering who they’re facing. That’s 10 gone, 22 to go.

They’re Too Bad

You can face the worst team in all of football, but if you’re the second-worst team, well, I’m still not going to be too excited about selecting you. We’ll return to the power rankings here and cross off any team in the bottom 12. Atlanta Falcons (@ Green Bay) Carolina Panthers (@ Cleveland) Cleveland Browns (vs. Carolina) Las Vegas Raiders (@ New Orleans) New York Giants (vs. Tennessee) New York Jets (@ Detroit) Tampa Bay Buccaneers (vs. Minnesota) Tennessee Titans (@ NY Giants) Eight more eliminations leaves us with 14 remaining. Want more tools and analysis to keep you alive in your survivor pool? Check out PoolGenius for all the best offerings.

Island Games

Island games just get weird. I would need some very convincing evidence to pick anyone on a Thursday, or a Monday, or (we’ll get to them) an overseas 9 a.m. ET game. There aren’t many left this week, but I still want to note them. Chicago Bears (vs. Philadelphia) Green Bay Packers (vs. Atlanta) Philadelphia Eagles (@ Chicago) Three more gone, 11 left.

They Have the Same Record

This one is a little silly, but I’m actually comfortable with it. It’s Week 3. It’s too early to have grand conclusions on teams. So I’m not saying a 1-1 team is a true .500 club or an 0-2 team is a true .000 team or anything like that. That would be silly. But what I am saying is, at this point in the season, I would feel dumb if I picked a 1-1 team against a 1-1 team and was like, “Well this 1-1 team is obviously better,” and then I go out there and lose with that 1-1 team. So these are soft eliminations, and I’ll still consider them for Honorable Mention below, but as far as my No. 1 pick goes, anyone facing a team with the same record as it is out. Baltimore Ravens (@ Dallas) Detroit Lions (vs. NY Jets) Houston Texans (@ Indianapolis) Indianapolis Colts (vs. Houston) That’s four more, leaving seven behind — our seven contenders.

The Contenders

Once we’re down to this small a number of teams, we’re done cutting them in swaths. We look at the pros and cons for each team and then figure it out. I’m also diving into our NFL Betting Model to see what the numbers think of the game.

Buffalo Bills (vs. LA Chargers)

Model Projection: Bills 28.27-21.66, Bills 66.1% win rate

Pros: The Chargers have been a disaster, and the Bills have been off to a great start. Cons: LA has to start getting better at some point, right?

Cincinnati Bengals (@ Pittsburgh)

Model Projection: Steelers 22.99-22.43, Bengals 48.5% win rate Pros: The Bengals are off to their best start in years, the defense actually looks competent, and the Steelers are a mess. Cons: Confidently picking anyone in an AFC North matchup has historically not been a wise decision.

Kansas City Chiefs (@ Miami)

Model Projection: Chiefs 27.01-19.46, Chiefs 69.4% win rate Pros: The Chiefs are off to a very good start, while the Dolphins are off to the exact start we all expected. Cons: Maybe you don’t want to take a team on the road? That’s all I got.

Minnesota Vikings (@ Tampa Bay)

Model Projection: Buccaneers 21.18-20.43, Vikings 47.7% win rate Pros: The Vikings are 2-0 despite a mess at quarterback and shut down the Bears offense. Cons: The mess at quarterback persists — Kyler Murray is back this week, but we haven’t seen anything from him yet.

New Orleans (vs. Las Vegas)

Model Projection: Saints 21.30-16.19, Saints 66.5% win rate Pros: The Saints are a two-point conversion away from 2-0, and Tyler Shough leads the league in passing yards. Cons: The 2-0 Raiders … might actually be good? At the least, they aren’t the pushover we thought they’d be.

San Francisco 49ers (vs. Arizona)

Model Projection: 49ers 25.78-21.67, 49ers 60.7% win rate Pros: No team has been more dominant through two weeks, with the 49ers rolling the Rams and Dolphins. Cons: It’s possible beating a team off an around-the-world flight and the tanking Dolphins isn’t actually that impressive. Meanwhile, the 49ers are getting hurt like crazy.

Seattle Seahawks (@ Washington)

Model Projection: Seahawks 27.07-19.04, Seahawks 70.7% win rate Pros: Let’s see … the Seahawks are 2-0 in convincing fashion despite losing their quarterback, while Washington is 0-2 and lost their quarterback. Cons: Uh… cross-country tip? Hard to really have much of a reason here.

The Pick

Seattle Seahawks (@ Washington)

Loathe as I am to take a team on the road, the Seahawks and Chiefs are pretty clearly the best options this week and both are on the road. So we’ll take Seattle against Marcus Mariota in his 2026 starting debut against the defending Super Bowl champion. Jaxon Smith-Njigba might go for 200 yards in this one.

Honorable Mention

Kansas City Chiefs (@ Miami) San Francisco 49ers (vs. Arizona) 2026 record: 1-1 Week 1: Chargers (L) Week 2: Eagles (W) Week 3: Seahawks

item.title: Tyler Shough looks like he really could be the Saints’ QB of the future
item.description: Mike Tyson famously said that everyone has a plan until they get punched in the mouth. For Tyler Shough, that might just be the plan. Shough and the New Orleans Saints are 1-1, with both games following a similar format. The Saints go down early as Shough struggles, but then catch fire late to force […]
item.content:encoded:
Mike Tyson famously said that everyone has a plan until they get punched in the mouth.

For Tyler Shough, that might just be the plan.

Shough and the New Orleans Saints are 1-1, with both games following a similar format. The Saints go down early as Shough struggles, but then catch fire late to force a dramatic conclusion. In Week 1, the Saints trailed the Detroit Lions 21-7 late in the third quarter, before forcing overtime on the road. New Orleans had two chances to steal the win late, only to see a 62-yard field goal attempt from Daniel Carlson sail wide right at the end of regulation, and a two-point attempt in overtime come up empty, leaving the final scorer 31-30 in favor of Detroit.

Then in Week 2, Shough and the Saints trailed the Baltimore Ravens 17-9 as the fourth quarter began, but used 15-unanswered points to g o into Baltimore and defeat the Ravens by a final score of 24-17.

Yes, there was a somewhat controversial ruling on a fourth-down touchdown sneak from Shough with under two minutes remaining, but the ruling stood, and the Saints were suddenly 1-1.

Shough’s own production has followed that same pattern: Start slow, end red-hot. Against the Lions in Week 1, Shough was 10-for-22 for 85 yards and an interception in the first half against Detroit, but completed 25-of-34 passes for 325 yards and three touchdowns, along with an interception, over the second half and into overtime.

Against Baltimore in Week 2, Shough connected on 12-of-15 passes for 102 yards in the first half, but connected on 15-of-19 passes for 150 yards and a touchdown in the second half.

Isolating just the fourth quarter this season, Shough has completed 24-of-31 passes for 277 yards and two touchdowns this season, without an interception. That is good for an NFL Passer Rating of 125.3, and an Adjusted Net Yards per Attempt of 9.59.

NFL league averages in those two categories are 94.7 and 6.4, respectively.

While you never apologize for wins in the NFL, and a 1-1 start has the Saints right in the mix of things in the NFC South, Saints fans are rightfully asking: Is this sustainable?

Given what we have seen, it just might be.

Certainly teams do not want to build the entire season out of comebacks and fourth quarters alone, but there is something of a roadmap for the 2026 Saints to follow if they try and do just that. That roadmap? The 2025 Chicago Bears, who rode seven comeback wins — six in the regular season and one more on Wild Card Weekend — to the Divisional Round a year ago.

Returning to Shough, some of his best moments this year, from a film perspective, have come in these fourth-quarter comebacks. Take this fourth-down conversion against the Lions to extend a drive:

Detroit brings a blitz off the right edge, and it leads to a free runner at the quarterback. But Shough deftly steps up in the pocket and around the pressure, before firing a strike to rookie wide receiver Bryce Lance to move the chains. Perhaps the best part of this play? The ball security. As he steps up in the pocket Shough keeps both hands glued to the football, which prevents a potential strip-sack as Roger McCreary manages to get a hand on Shough as he blitzes off the edge.

Then there was this deep shot to Chris Olave, with Shough staring down yet another free runner:

Detroit uses a stunt off the right side of the offense to spring Aidan Hutchinson free, but Shough has the toughness — both physical and mental — to stare down the free runner and deliver this downfield throw to Olave, who finishes the play through contact himself to give the Saints a first down inside the red zone with under two minutes remaining.

Again, this trend of Shough stepping up in the big moments continued last Sunday. Take this touchdown to Olave, as he hits the wide receiver on a dig route with pristine timing and anticipation:

More than anything else, it is this read and throw that gives me the belief that Shough’s fourth-quarter prowess will not only continue, but grow into the rest of the game script. As we talked about earlier this week regarding another young NFC South quarterback, Bryce Young, timing and anticipation are the tell-tale signs that the game is slowing down for a quarterback.

Here, Shough confirms the split-field coverage and comes right to Olave on his in-breaking route. I love the decision, the timing, and the anticipation on this touchdown throw. This is a confident and decisive quarterback, trusting his view of the field, his read of the coverage, and the concept at his fingertips.

Confident and decisive quarterbacks are successful ones.

That is certainly sustainable.

item.title: How the Denver Broncos can beat the Los Angeles Rams on Sunday Night Football
item.description: Here is what the Denver Broncos have to accomplish to defeat the Los Angeles Rams on Sunday Night Football.
item.content:encoded:
The Denver Broncos are coming off an impressive Week 2 victory over the Jacksonville Jaguars. Their Week 3 opponent is the Los Angeles Rams, who earned a decisive victory over the New York Giants on Monday Night Football. They will be another tough opponent in Denver’s gridiron gauntlet to start the season. Here is what the Broncos need to do to beat the Rams on Sunday Night Football.

Do what you can to slow down Matthew Stafford

At 38 years of age, Matthew Stafford is in his eighteenth season in the NFL. Interestingly enough, the Broncos have only faced him twice. Both of those matchups were when he was playing the Detroit Lions.

In 2025, Stafford had a career year with 4,707 passing yards and 46 touchdowns. Those marks topped the NFL and earned him a Pro-Bowl nod, a first-team All-Pro honor, and the first MVP award of his historic career. He had a rough start to his 2026 season against the San Francisco 49ers in Week 1. However, the longtime veteran played much better against the Giants and was 22-of-31 for 327 yards with 4 touchdowns and 1 interception.

Defensive Coordinator Vance Joseph had a tremendous gameplan to combat Trevor Lawrence and the high-powered Jacksonville Jaguars defense in Week 2. Joseph and his players will have to execute well again in order for the Broncos to earn a primetime victory Sunday night. Stafford was without star wide receiver Puka Nacua on MNF, but if he is available for SNF, that will make this task even harder.

Keep committed to the running game

It wasn’t an easy, but the Broncos were able to top the 100-yard mark with their rushing attack last weekend against the Jaguars. That was without RJ Harvey who missed the game with a hamstring injury and J.K. Dobbins for most of the second half.

In turn, the Broncos looked to rookie running back Jonah Coleman late in the game. The fourth-round draft pick had several key runs, including the go-ahead touchdown to cement a victory for Denver. He displayed tremendous patience, vision, and nose for the endzone in his small sample size.

It’s too early to know whether Harvey or Dobbins will suit up on Sunday. Though Head Coach Sean Payton remained optimistic at that possibility in his Monday morning presser. Regardless, Offensive Coordinator Davis Webb needs to commit to the run game.

The Rams’ defensive front will be without Myles Garrett which should help in this matter. Against the 49ers, the Rams struggled to stop Kyle Shanahan’s rushing attack and gave up 174 yards on the ground. Though against the Giants, they performed much better and allowed just 52 yards on the ground.

The Broncos had a lot of success in heavier personnel and running the ball under center in the second half versus the Jaguars. Let’s see more of that moving forward. A strong rushing attack will be essential to control the clock and limit the opportunities Stafford and the Rams have on offense.

Operate better on third down and perform better in the red zone

Two issues have been constant for the Broncos’ offense in their first two games of the season: struggling to convert on third down and missing opportunities in the redzone. To be competitive on Sunday Night Football and compete at a high level throughout the entire season, both of these issues need to be corrected.

The Broncos have converted just 6 of 23 third down attempts this season. Meanwhile, they are just 3 of 7 in the redzone. A big part of this can also be attributed Denver’s ongoing penchant for penalties. Denver has seventeen thus far, which makes them one of the most penalized teams in the NFL.

This is an area the team has to get much better at. They can’t settle for field goals or turn the ball over in the redzone. They also can’t afford to keep having so many three-and-outs. I don’t want to see Denver have to try and rally back or outduel Stafford in a shootout. Improvement and efficiency in these areas will be an absolute must for the Broncos to earn their second win of the year.

item.title: Life after Jaxson Dart: How can the NY Giants adapt to losing their QB?
item.description: How can the NY Giants adjust after losing Jaxson Dart for the year?
item.content:encoded:
The New York Giants have to adapt to a new reality after the injury quarterback Jaxson Dart suffered against the Los Angeles Rams.

What was originally believed to be a relatively minor injury from which he could return by the Giants’ bye week turned into season-ender. Dart will need surgery to repair his PCL and meniscus.

Now, the Giants have to reckon with life without their starting quarterback. And while the Giants’ immediate concern is the Tennessee Titans, they now know that they won’t see Dart again as their starting quarterback until OTAs in 2027.

The implications have been coming in waves as we learn more about his status.

We spent months speculating on how Matt Nagy, Greg Roman, and Brian Callahan would combine their philosophies to build the Giants’ offense. The Giants’ offensive scheme was impressive against the Dallas Cowboys and was clearly built around Dart’s manifold skillset.

Dart is not only an accurate passer with the ability to make impressive throws from the pocket and off-platform, he’s also a great athlete who can extend, scramble, or gash the defense as a runner himself. It’s a skill set which which John Harbaugh was excited to work, as he said back in July.

“Jaxson’s capable of doing a lot of things,” Harbaugh said on ‘The Domonique Foxworth Show.’ “Like he can live in a lot of different worlds, football-wise. He can live in a power-running game, obviously, and a power-running game protects the quarterback because you can hand the ball off and make people defend that and keep them honest. Then, it opens up your play-action passing game. … That stuff, we’re gonna be in those worlds.

“But now we can also get in the gun or we can get in the pistol, and we can run RPOs, we can run quarterback-driven runs with Jaxson Dart, a lot of the stuff that we hand in Baltimore with Lamar, as well.

…

“So, that all kind of goes together on first and second down to create problems for the defense, and I just feel like it all starts with the quarterback. Jaxson is a guy that does give you a chance to live in all those different worlds. So, if he can do it, then we’re gonna do it, and that’s what we’re planning on doing.”

The Giants might have planned to live in those different worlds, but the injury to Dart came along like the Death Star and those worlds went the way of Alderaan.

Jameis Winston is a talented thrower of the ball, with a powerful arm and the ability to attack all areas of the field. He may be prone to interceptions, but that has more to do with a willingness to challenge any receiving window than a lack of accuracy as a passer.

However, he simply doesn’t have anything like Dart’s athleticism, and the loss of Dart’s mobility has ripped pages out of the Giants’ playbook.

The Giants’ offense in Week 1 had Roman’s finger prints all over it, as well as those of Nagy. Roman has long coached mobile quarterbacks and freely incorporates their athleticism in his run schemes. He coached Alex Smith and Collin Kaepernick under Jim Harbaugh with the San Francisco 49ers, Lamar Jackson with the Baltimore Ravens, and Justin Herbert with the Los Angeles Chargers.

Nagy, too, has enjoyed mobile quarterbacks. He coached Alex Smith and Patrick Mahomes with the Kansas City Chiefs, and then Mitchell Trubisky and Justin Fields with the Chicago Bears.

Mobile quarterbacks are the bane of defensive coordinators. Their ability to move the pocket, as well as extend and scramble, slow down the opposing pass rush and force the defense to play contain. Their ability to contribute in the run game stresses perimeter players and linebackers, making play-action all the more effective, because any mesh-point could turn into a quarterback run.

Roman has also used his quarterbacks’ athleticism as a counter-punch for the power run game, giving added dimensions to stress the defense.

And while Jameis may have a receiving touchdown on his resume, those “dual threat” aspects aren’t present in his game.

The Giants will likely have to shift to a more traditional offensive scheme with Winston under center. The good news is that Brian Callahan has experience with a less mobile, pass-first quarterback in Joe Burrow, while tight ends coach Tim Kelly was the Giants’ interim offensive coordinator a year ago. Kelly’s experience coaching Winston as the starting quarterback when Dart missed a pair of games with a concussion will be invaluable now. Meanwhile, Callahan’s background in the “New West Coast” offense (such as is run by Kyle Shanahan, Sean McVay, and Klint Kubiak) could give the offense a way forward.

That could mean taking a page out of Sean McVay’s book with Matthew Stafford, who is in a similar mold as Winston (though a far better quarterback).

The Rams use alignment, spacing, and personnel to hide their intentions, pairing heavy packages with precision route concepts, and light packages with the run. The Giants already have similar concepts in their offense, but could better tailor them to Winston’s talents. In particular, they could look to use heavy packages and play-action to open up explosive passes to players like Malik Nabers, Isaiah Likely, and Darnell Mooney. That, in turn, could open up the run game as defenses are stressed vertically by Winston’s penchant to attack deep.

On the flip side, the Giants could lean into lighter personnel packages with Cam Skattebo or Najee Harris in the backfield. Teams could follow the Giants into lighter personnel packages, and be more vulnerable to Greg Roman’s power run schemes.

It’s possible that the Giants could look to restructure their roster slightly to better fit Winston’s skill set as the weeks go on. However, their team is their team at this point. And while the Giants will undoubtedly “look at all options”, they’re unlikely to acquire any game-changing players midseason.

Final thoughts

No team plans to be without their starting quarterback for most of the season. It’s one thing to be without Dart for a game or three, but it’s quite another to be without him for 15 games.

The Giants extended Winston to the tune of $13 million for a reason. They clearly believe that Winston is one of the best backup quarterbacks in the NFL. He played poorly against the Rams, however the entire team seemed to be in disarray after Dart’s injuries. The hope is that he’ll play like the quarterback Giants believe him to be with actual practice reps with the starting offense and the knowledge that he’s The Guy going forward.

They also count Winston as a leader in the locker room, and are now counting on the charismatic veteran to rally his teammates.

In other words, the Giants are depending on Jameis Winston and need him to show up, as well as support him to the best of their ability. That might not preclude them from trying to procure another quarterback if they don’t love the idea of Jake Haener being their backup for the next 15 games.

It also now falls to Harbaugh to prove that he is worth his $100 million contract and be the experienced, steady hand to see the Giants through the storm. Likewise, Joe Schoen now needs to prove himself worth his extension and continue to explore all options to give Harbaugh and Winston the best tools possible to make the best of a bad situation.

The Giants’ new reality is that they need to adapt on the fly to winning with a different brand of football than they intended a week ago.

item.title: Steelers’ offensive line decisions continue to plague struggling offense
item.description: The Steelers’ offensive line is the root of the offense’s issues.
item.content:encoded:
The Pittsburgh Steelers’ offensive line decisions continue to be puzzling. Like a simplified 24-piece puzzle that’s scrambled into 1,000. They just can’t get it right.

42-year-old Aaron Rodgers was constantly under pressure when the Steelers lost 20-3 to the New England Patriots. Better defenses await in the following weeks. The problems didn’t begin when the first snap hit Rodgers’ hands against the Falcons two weeks ago, but date back to the first day Mike McCarthy was hired.

McCarthy and Omar Khan’s plan for the offensive line didn’t make sense from the start. Pittsburgh decided to move starting right guard Mason McCormick and right tackle Troy Fautanu to the left side of the line at the start of offseason workouts. What seemed like a confusing move has resulted in someone falling asleep on their keyboard, pressing the “Q” button with the number of questions that ensued. Why? Was it necessary? Did it make sense?

In theory, the decision made sense… on paper. Fautanu played left tackle at Washington, and McCormick played left guard at South Dakota State. You’d think a former first-round pick in Fautanu would adapt back to the position he’s comfortable with, but this isn’t Kansas anymore, Toto. 

Life in the NFL at the tackle spots is different from college, ask Broderick Jones. How’d that one turn out? Dan Moore was seemingly incapable of playing the right side and forced Jones to a position he wasn’t comfortable with. Has the new staff made better choices with the line than Mike Tomlin’s? It seems like the decisions are coming from inside the front office – hello, Khan and Andy Weidl. Keeping the cohesion with Fautanu and McCormick made sense, but if it’s not broken, why try to fix it?

The Steelers had a stable right side of the offensive line intact for years to come, but made a non-problem a glaring weakness. Former seventh-round pick and swing tackle Spencer Anderson has been tasked with holding down the fort at right guard. The fort was ransacked and overtaken by the Patriots on Sunday. Anderson allowed seven pressures against New England in Foxboro, the most of any right guard in football last week. The Patriots sacked Rodgers four times and forced two fumbles, one resulting in a scoop-and-score. He’s been sacked six times and pressured on 29 drop-backs through two games.

Right tackle Dylan Cook did a decent job replacing Jones last season on the left side and became the leader in the clubhouse to start at right. He’s allowed more defenders to easily move past him than a PNC Park turnstile on bobblehead night. 

It’s not just the 29th-ranked passing game (175 yards per game) that’s struggled. The Steelers are only averaging 74.5 yards per game on the ground, also 29th in the league, and are 30th in total yards. Mike McCarthy’s offense has scored 16 points through his first two games. Matt Canada’s unit scored 33. Arthur Smith’s offense scored 31. Not a good look for the Steelers’ first offensive head coach in over 50 years. 

Center Zach Frazier is the only holdover from the 2025 offensive line. First-round pick Max Iheanachor dealt with an injury in training camp that hampered his development, but it’s beyond time we see what the rookie out of Arizona State has to offer the team. The Steelers placed themselves in a difficult position by picking Iheanachor and only committing him to the right side, partly resulting in the shift in dynamics. Wouldn’t it have been easier to change one thing (Iheanachor at left) than two? 

The lack of cohesion during camp was startling and is likely playing a factor for offensive line coach James Campen. Pittsburgh rotated Anderson and Brock Hoffman at right guard, plus Cook, Jones, and Iheanachor at right tackle before training Jones at the end of preseason. If you want everyone on the same page, why not keep them together for every rep and workout?

The game of musical chairs continued with the Steelers rotating Anderson and Cook between the left and right sides during the media viewing window of practice on Wednesday. Hoffman and Iheanachor both worked exclusively on the right. They are trying to clean up their own mess and fix gaps in pre-snap communication deeper than Pittsburgh potholes in December.

Time is ticking on how long Rodgers can hold up and prevent getting hurt behind this unit after taking nasty hits against the Patriots. Can it possibly get worse? I’m afraid to even ask.

item.title: Week 3 NFL Survivor strategy and picks with safe, value, and trap picks
item.description: David Fucillo provides NFL Survivor pool tips in Week 3, offering up safe, value, and trap picks.
item.content:encoded:
The NFL heads into Week 3 as autumn has officially arrived. We have one last week in September and we’ve already got plenty of chaos in the NFL. I don’t think anybody was prediction a 2-0 Raiders squad, and even 2-0 Vikings is catching me off guard. On the other hand, I definitely wasn’t expecting 0-2 starts by the Chargers or Buccaneers. There’s a long way to go, but it’s getting wild already!

I’m back with another round of Survivor picks. You pick one team each week to win. If they win you advance, if they lose you’re out in most cases. I’m in one pool with four entries, but it’s also a double-elimination pool. I managed to get one of my entries eliminated in two weeks after taking the Chargers in Week 1 and the Bucs in Week 2. Another entry has me down a strike after the Bucs loss last week (I took the Steelers in Week 1). My other two entries remain fully alive having gone Jaguars/Eagles with one and Raiders/49ers with the other.

Below I’ve got a look at the safest choices, best value picks, and then trap picks. I’ll post my own picks at the end. Since I publish this article on Thursday, I’ll update on Sunday once I lock in my three picks.

I’ve included odds for the favorite in each game, courtesy of FanDuel.

Safest picks

Chiefs (-11.5) over Dolphins

Kansas City is headed on the road, but Miami stinks. You’re probably better off saving the Chiefs for later in the season, but you can do worse than using them this week.

Best value picks

Packers (-5.5) over Falcons

The Packers haven’t impressed thus far, but the Falcons are truly awful. The one concern is that Michael Penix improves things, but Falcons fans aren’t particularly high on him on their own. I was leaning toward listing this as a trap game given the QB change and it’s a short week game, but I’m that low on Atlanta.

Trap pick

Bills (-7) over Chargers
Seahawks (-7) over Commanders

I think Buffalo and Seattle both win, but these games are just a little bit tricky. LA has been a huge underachiever this season, but they have the talent to turn it around. The Bills are a touchdown favorite, but you’re better saving them for Week 14 against the Dolphins.

The Commanders lost Jayden Daniels to a dislocated elbow and it’s Marcus Mariota time. He’s nothing special, but with Seattle traveling cross-country for a 1 p.m. ET start, it’s probably best to skip this one. You can save the Seahawks for Week 9 at home against the Cardinals or Week 14 at home against the Giants.

My picks this week

I’ll be using the Chiefs to some degree this week. The other two weeks I’d use them at this point are Week 9 vs. the Jets and Week 11 vs. the Cardinals. Both weeks I can find comparable or better options. I’m also leaning 49ers over Cardinals with one of my picks. They’re playing well, but similarly have enough tough games that I’m comfortable passing on them later. I’m tempted by the Packers, but they get the Dolphins at home in Week 15. Who knows if I’ll make it that far, but I’m willing to wait.

item.title: AFC North Week 2 Recap: 2-0 Bengals alone atop division
item.description: The Bengals take first place in the AFC North.
item.content:encoded:
Week 2 of the 2026 NFL season is in the books. Only one team remains undefeated in the AFC North after just two games.

Cincinnati Bengals (2-0)

The Bengals are now the lone undefeated team in the division after a 20-6 victory over the Houston Texans.

Cincinnati’s revamped defense had another strong outing in Week 2. Spearheaded by defensive tackle Dexter Lawrence, the unit held the Texans’ running backs to just 18 rushing yards. Demetrius Knight Jr. led the team with 12 total tackles. The Bengals sacked C.J. Stroud four times, with two coming from Cedric Johnson. Cincinnati could be one of the top teams in the AFC if their defense can continue to play near this level.

The highlight for the Bengals’ offense was Ja’Marr Chase and his two touchdowns. The superstar receiver’s first touchdown catch was particularly impressive as he contorted his body to reel in the pass.

Chase finished with seven catches for 75 yards and two scores while his running mate Tee Higgins led the way with 95 yards on five targets. Chase Brown led the ground attack with 80 yards on 20 carries. Joe Burrow completed 20 of 31 passes for 207 yards and two touchdowns. Burrow’s back was a concern entering the game before being sacked five times by Houston’s defense. He admitted it was a little sore after the game, but that he was “good to go.” Given Burrow’s injury history, his back tightness will likely remain a talking point each week.

Baltimore Ravens (1-1)

The Ravens experienced the first disappointment of the Jesse Minter era with a 27-17 loss to the New Orleans Saints in the team’s home opener.

Baltimore’s defense found itself in an all-too-familiar position with their backs against the wall in the fourth quarter after blowing a double-digit lead. Similar to many of those prior instances, the unit was unable to get the game-sealing stop. Tyler Shough had little trouble marching down the field with the game on the line before scoring on a quarterback sneak. The Ravens sacked Shough just three times despite constant blitzes and his starting left tackle leaving the game due to an ankle injury.

Baltimore’s offense shoulders blame as well after scoring just three points in the second half. The offense had the ball for four drives in the second half, two of which were three-and-outs while the final ended in an interception. Lamar Jackson was solid for much of the day, completing 21 of 31 passes for 235 yards and a touchdown before the game-losing interception on the final drive. Rashod Bateman led the team with 88 receiving yards and a touchdown on seven catches in Zay Flowers’ absence. Derrick Henry finished the game with 68 rushing yards and a touchdown on 16 carries, with just five carries in the second half.

Pittsburgh Steelers (1-1)

The Steelers dropped to 1-1 with a 20-3 loss to the reigning AFC champion New England Patriots.

The decision to run it back another year with 42-year-old Aaron Rodgers at quarterback is looking questionable, to say the least, through two games of the season. Pittsburgh’s offense has scored just one touchdown through two games with the future Hall of Famer under center. Rodgers completed 23 of 39 passes against the Patriots for 187 yards and an interception while being sacked four times and losing a fumble. D.K. Metcalf, whom the Steelers acquired for a second-round pick and awarded a massive contract to a year ago, has had a rough start to the season, hauling in four catches for just 27 yards against New England. Germie Bernard was the leading receiver with 35 yards on four catches. Jaylen Warren led the rushing attack with 43 yards on 11 carries. Rico Dowdle left the game with a toe injury after carrying the ball seven times for 22 yards.

Pittsburgh’s defense did what it could by forcing two turnovers: an interception by Patrick Queen and a forced fumble on Rhamondre Stevenson by Nick Herbig. The defense sacked Drake Maye three times, with T.J. Watt accounting for 1.5 sacks. There is only so much the talented unit can do with so little help from the Steelers’ offense at the moment.

Cleveland Browns (1-1)

The Browns got their first win of the season on Sunday with a 23-19 victory over the Tampa Bay Buccaneers.

After a rough start to the season in Week 1, Deshaun Watson rebounded with a solid day against the Buccaneers, completing 24 of 30 pass attempts for 238 yards and two touchdowns while avoiding any turnovers. The biggest play of the day for Cleveland’s offense once again came from rookie Denzel Boston, as the second-round receiver scored a 55-yard touchdown. Boston finished the game with 95 yards to go with his one score on five catches. The run game was quiet for the Browns as Deshaun Watson led the team with 22 rushing yards on seven carries.

Cleveland’s defense faced a familiar foe in former Cleveland quarterback Baker Mayfield, picking him off once and sacking him three times. Carson Schwesinger led the unit with 10 total tackles. Jared Verse, acquired in the blockbuster trade that sent Myles Garrett to the Los Angeles Rams, has yet to make his impact felt in two games with his new team.

item.title: Falcons vs. Packers: What will Week 3’s win or loss mean for Atlanta?
item.description: A win will get this season back on track a bit, while a loss all but ends Atlanta’s hopes of a quality 2026.
item.content:encoded:
We’ve barely begun the season, yet the Falcons are already reeling following back to back weeks with Cooper Rush as the starter. The latest, a 34-3 home opener humiliation at the hands of the division rival Panthers, prompted a rain of boos from a frustrated fanbase.

Next for the Falcons is the start of three consecutive prime time matchups, starting with a trip to Lambeau Field to face the Green Bay Packers, who have gotten off to a disappointing start in their own right. The good news for the Falcons is that Michael Penix Jr. has been announced as the starter for that game, as he will make his highly anticipated season debut.

It’s a short week, and the Birds have no time to lick their wounds after the mauling they just took at the hands of the Panthers. The entire country will have a chance to watch Atlanta, who kick off Week 3 on Thursday Night Football.

Here is the scenario the Falcons face if they beat the Green Bay Packers in Week 3, as well as if they lose.

If the Falcons win

It will be a much needed bounce back and will work to regain the confidence of what looks to be a broken fanbase. Not that anybody at Flowery Branch seems to or should care about media narratives, but it will give them some positive PR after weeks of getting crushed by the media.

The team would finally have some liftoff, and could in theory find themselves tied for the division lead if all other scores around the NFC South work in their favor (however, they will remain at best in third place due to early season tiebreakers).

This would be a big blow dealt to the Packers, who would fall to 1-2 in a season of expectations. Atlanta would pull very close to .500 in their all time history against Green Bay, as the mark would be 18-19. They would also get a massive confidence boost going into the Monday night grudge match against the New Orleans Saints next week.

If the Falcons lose

This train will begin derailing not too far from the starting station, as the Birds will fall to 0-3 with the hard part of their schedule still lingering in the near future. The vibes around the fanbase will continue to sink as next week’s Monday Night Football game against the Saints will really turn into a must win. In truth, even if they win that one it may not make much of a difference long term after an 0-3 start.

As for the early division race, Atlanta could find themselves a quick 2.0 games behind both Carolina and New Orleans (who will both likely be favored in their matchups this weekend). Tampa will also be ahead of Atlanta even if they also lose and fall to 0-3, due to the divisional record tiebreaker, keeping the Falcons in the cellar of the NFC South for yet another week.

It’s a lot earlier than expected but we will likely need to begin tracking draft standings in this article series as early as next week.

item.title: Rooting against the AFC East is easy. The rest of Week 3 comes with conditions
item.description: The AFC East can keep losing. For everyone else, our Week 3 loyalties come with conditions.
item.content:encoded:
Buffalo did its part last week. Asking the rest of the NFL to cooperate apparently was a little too much. 

Still, the Bills head into Week 3 with two wins and a chance to add another against the Los Angeles Chargers on Sunday. That’s the assignment that matters most. Everything else is us being helpful — whether the teams involved appreciate our very temporary support or not. 

We’re three weeks into this, and our rooting interests already need a reminder: We don’t want every AFC team losing every week. Some of them need to win just enough to stay away from the best players in next year’s draft. 

The exception, of course, is the AFC East. The Patriots, Jets, and Dolphins can keep losing. We’ll live with the consequences. 

For everyone else, there’s an order to this. Buffalo wins first. Division rivals lose. Then we want wins from teams the Bills have beaten to help their strength of victory, followed by wins from other Buffalo opponents to build strength of schedule. When none of those apply, we want the AFC leaders coming back toward the middle of the standings and the struggling teams winning their way out of premium draft position. 

These are rooting interests, not predictions, and absolutely none of them require us to like the teams we’re choosing. Which is good, because you’ve probably already noticed who Miami plays this week. 

_____________________________________________________________________________

AFC EAST 

Buffalo Bills over Los Angeles Chargers 

We wanted the Chargers to win last week. This week, they’re visiting Buffalo, so that arrangement is over. The Bills have an opportunity to get to 3-0, and nothing happening elsewhere makes up for letting that opportunity get away. Go Bills!

Jacksonville Jaguars over New England Patriots 

Before anyone brings up the fact that Buffalo plays New England twice, yes, we know. That’s why the division rule comes before strength of schedule. Jacksonville gets our support, and the Patriots get another week of us wishing them absolutely nothing good. 

Detroit Lions over New York Jets 

Detroit can help us twice here. Buffalo already beat the Lions, so a Detroit win adds to the Bills’ strength of victory while handing the Jets a loss. We spent last Thursday rooting against them, but this is a very good week to get back on Detroit’s side. 

Kansas City Chiefs over Miami Dolphins 

Yes, again. But this week, you don’t even have to listen to a lengthy explanation about Buffalo’s schedule. Kansas City is playing Miami, and our division rule settles it. You can spend the entire game complaining about the Chiefs and still want the Dolphins to lose. We’re capable of both. 

_____________________________________________________________________________

The rest of the AFC 

Houston Texans over Indianapolis Colts 

Houston, we need you to start holding up your end of this arrangement. Buffalo already has the win over the Texans. Now we need Houston to collect some wins of their own so that victory can help the Bills in a tiebreaker later. 

Pittsburgh Steelers over Cincinnati Bengals 

Neither team is on Buffalo’s schedule, so this one goes to the standings. Cincinnati has started 2-0, while Pittsburgh is 1-1. Give the Steelers the win and bring the Bengals back to the middle of the pack. We don’t need Cincinnati building an early cushion while we’re busy worrying about everybody else. 

Cleveland Browns over Carolina Panthers 

This is where our draft-position rule gets some work. Neither team is a Buffalo opponent, and Cleveland isn’t leading its division. Let the Browns collect a win that could eventually move them away from a premium pick, while the Panthers take the loss. If somebody is going to come out of this season with access to the best available talent in next year’s draft, we’d prefer that somebody live in the NFC. 

Tennessee Titans over New York Giants 

Same principle. The Titans are winless, and neither team is on Buffalo’s schedule. We don’t need Tennessee spending the entire season working toward the top of the draft. Give the Titans a win and leave the Giants a little closer to that particular prize. 

Las Vegas Raiders over New Orleans Saints 

Here’s where the order of our rules matters. We could make an argument for wanting an AFC loss, but Las Vegas is on Buffalo’s schedule, and New Orleans isn’t. For now, that strength-of-schedule benefit gets the Raiders our support. If the conference race gives us a more pressing reason to root against them later, we’ll adjust, but we aren’t there yet. 

Baltimore Ravens over Dallas Cowboys 

Baltimore is another Buffalo opponent, so we’re sticking with the schedule benefit here, too. There will probably be plenty of opportunities to root against the Ravens before this is over. This week, we want them beating Dallas. Nobody said following our own rules would always be pleasant. 

Los Angeles Rams over Denver Broncos 

Buffalo plays both teams, which means we get the same strength-of-schedule benefit either way. Denver won its division last season, so this is a chance to apply our rule about bringing those teams down a peg without giving up anything on the schedule side. 

_____________________________________________________________________________

NFC vs. NFC games 

Green Bay Packers over Atlanta Falcons 

The Packers are on Buffalo’s schedule, and the Falcons aren’t. That gives us a straightforward assignment for Thursday night without needing to consult the standings, think about the draft, or argue with ourselves. Go Pack Go. 

Minnesota Vikings over Tampa Bay Buccaneers 

Minnesota gets the same treatment. The Bills play the Vikings later this season, so we want them adding wins whenever Buffalo isn’t the opponent. Tampa Bay doesn’t give us that benefit. Go Vikings. 

Chicago Bears over Philadelphia Eagles 

Last week, I let my irritation with the Bears’ offense comparisons help settle a pick between two Buffalo opponents. This week, only Chicago is on the Bills’ schedule, so I have to put that aside. We’re rooting for the Bears. After all, having rules means being held to them. 

San Francisco 49ers over Arizona Cardinals 

San Francisco has opened 2-0, while Arizona is 1-1. With no direct Buffalo schedule benefit available, we’ll give the win to the 49ers and leave the Cardinals closer to the better pick.  

_____________________________________________________________________________

So, yes, we’re asking some AFC teams to win and others to lose while making a few exceptions for Buffalo’s schedule. We want help now, useful tiebreakers later, and fewer opportunities for struggling conference opponents to solve their problems next April. 

If that sounds a little selfish, you’ve understood the assignment.  

Go Bills!

item.title: POLL: Should the Lions re-sign RB Jamaal Williams?
item.description: Jamaal Williams wants to return to the NFL and has interest in the Detroit Lions. Should they re-sign the veteran RB?
item.content:encoded:
On Wednesday, Dave Birkett of the Detroit Free Press dropped an article revealing that former Detroit Lions running back Jamaal Williams is attempting to make a comeback in the NFL after being out of the league in 2025. Williams told Birkett that he called up Lions coach Dan Campbell about a possible reunion with the team, but Campbell said they were sticking with the running backs they currently have at the moment.

Those running backs are Jahmyr Gibbs, Sione Vaki, and Jacob Saylors—with Jabari Small on the practice squad. While the Lions are down their initial backup running back in Isiah Pacheco, who is out until December with a back injury, Detroit has adjusted to that injury by increasing Gibbs’ overall role and using Vaki as the next man up. It may not have the flash of Sonic and Knuckles, but Gibbs has been effective and Vaki is growing into his role.

But Williams was undeniably an important piece of the offense in 2021 and 2022. Besides being a vocal leader and an entertaining personality, he was also a short-yardage and touchdown machine. In 2022, he set the franchise record for rushing touchdowns in a season (17) while also accumulating 1,000 yards rushing.

However, his career grinded to a halt when he left Detroit. He managed just 306 rushing yards and one touchdown with the Saints in 2023 (at just 2.9 YPC), then followed it up with 164 rushing yards in 2024. After a year away from the NFL, how much is left in the 31-year-old back?

So today’s Question of the Day is:

Do you want the Lions to sign Jamaal Williams?

My answer: The heart and the reporter side of me says emphatically yes. Williams was a character and a joy to chop it up with in the locker room. His addition would also make a very good story, and he’d be an endless fountain of good quotes. In short, he’d be good for business.

But as a football analyst, it’s hard for me to make a logical case here. While I’d like a more even split between Gibbs and the RB2 to ensure we’re still getting the best version of Gibbs in December and January… and in 2029, they have Vaki and Saylors for a reason. They still believe in Vaki as a potential offensive weapon, but he needs the reps and learning experiences. I thought he already made a nice jump from a rough Week 1 to a fairly solid Week 2.

The Lions rostered Vaki and Saylors not just for their special teams acumen, but because they believe in them as depth pieces behind Pacheco. As soon as Pacheco goes down, that doesn’t mean they have to completely change course. Trust your depth, and if they struggle or suffer another injury, then we can have a discussion about Williams. But, for now, I don’t really see a reason for adding a player who hasn’t been productive in the NFL since 2022—regardless of much I may admire him as a person.

item.title: Bills news: How Joe Brady is helping maximize Josh Allen
item.description: By calling more passing plays on early downs, Joe Brady is unleashing Josh Allen’s full potential for a potent offense.
item.content:encoded:
Through two weeks, Josh Allen and the Buffalo Bills have looked borderline unstoppable on offense, hanging 36 points on the Houston Texans—widely considered to be the top defense in the NFL—in Week 1 before pilling up 41 points on the Detroit Lions in Week 2.

Allen became the first player in league history to have at least five passing TDs and three rushing TDs through the first two games of a season, and as good as Allen has been to date in his NFL career, it seems that new Bills head coach/former offensive coordinator Joe Brady is helping unleash Allen’s full potential early in the 2026 NFL season.

After two weeks, today’s edition of Buffalo Rumblinks leads off by discussing how Brady is positioning Allen to thrive in this dynamic offense, including how the Bills are trusting Allen to do damage with his arm in first- and second-down situations.

Check out the assessments below and then let us know your thoughts in the comments section.

Bills are unleashing Josh Allen in early-down scenarios

Unlike in past years under former head coach Sean McDermott, when the tendency was for Buffalo to run the ball with dynamic running back James Cook on first down—including last year, when the Bills ran more than 50% of the time on first and second down—so far this year, Joe Brady has given Josh Allen the green light to attack downfield in early-down scenarios, and Bills fans have to love the results so far.

The Bills are throwing the ball more than 55% of the time on first and second down (eighth-most in the NFL) this year. In leading an offense that has scored touchdowns on 10 of its 18 possessions (not counting end of half kneel down situations), Brady is dialing up more passing plays on early downs, and those passing plays are taking place downfield and resulting in big chunk plays instead of bubble screens and checkdowns.

Through two games, Allen’s average depth of target (aDOT) is 10.5 yards, which puts him tied for third among all QBs this year and represents Allen’s highest aDOT since his 2018 rookie season and a marked improvement from last year’s 7.8 figure, the 11th-lowest among qualifying quarterbacks.

On the whole, Brady has called for passing plays on 57.9% of Buffalo’s offensive snaps (tied for 18th most), far more than the last year of McDermott’s tenure (54.1%, 30th in the NFL). And Allen is connecting more on those deep passes, ranking tied for third in completions of at least 20 yards with nine so far.

After tearing apart the Lions in Week 2, Allen’s stellar play netted him his 19th AFC Offensive Player of the Week honor of his career.

The Steelers barely beat an Atlanta Falcons team in Week 1 that’s probably going to finish as one of the worst teams this year based on how terrible their quarterback situation is. Then, in Week 2, the New England Patriots absolutely slapped the Steelers silly after being embarrassed in Week 1 by the Seattle Seahawks.

This team has some good players, but they have yet to really mesh through two weeks under new head coach Mike McCarthy. And it feels like with Aaron Rodgers already calling out the coaching staff, the wheels could come off sooner rather than later.

But this is a rivalry game, so nothing is off the table. If the Bengals offense can’t find more rhythm this week, it could be a long day in the Steel City. After all, the Texans defense just gave this offense fits for much of the game, largely because of the pass rush.

item.title: Where is Josh Jacobs? Latest news on Packers RB's court case
item.description: The Green Bay Packers will be without running back Josh Jacobs on "Thursday Night Football" as his legal case persists. What we know.
item.content:encoded:
The Green Bay Packers will be without their usual starting running back yet again in their Week 3 "Thursday Night Football" game.

Josh Jacobs remains on the commissioner's exempt list for a third game as his court case plays out. The eighth-year running back reached a plea deal earlier this month for two misdemeanor charges – one for battery, one for criminal damage to property – but the NFL's investigation is still ongoing.

Jacobs' two charges stemmed from an incident involving his ex-girlfriend in May and his subsequent arrest.

The NFL placed Jacobs on the commissioner's exempt list – a form of paid administrative leave – on Aug. 30. Players on the list are not allowed to practice or attend games, and time on the exempt list can count toward a suspension retroactively if the league hands down such a punishment after its investigation.

JOSH JACOBS: Packers RB reaches plea deal in battery case, NFL reviewing

One of the main reasons for the hold-up in determining disciplinary action against Jacobs is the league's desire to see a video of the incident that led to the running back's arrest. The victim, Jacobs' ex-girlfriend, has petitioned the court to permanently seal evidence from the case, including the video. Her attorneys argue the sealing of evidence is within her rights under Marsy's Law – a recently added amendment to Wisconsin's state constitution that gives additional rights to victims of a crime – to protect her privacy, dignity and safety.

Here's what to know:

Josh Jacobs update: Latest news from court case

Jacobs pleaded no contest to misdemeanor battery and criminal damage to property during a court appearance on Thursday, Sept. 10.

As part of an announced plea deal, the 28-year-old was found guilty on the charge of battery and ordered to pay a $1,000 fine plus costs.

For the second charge of criminal damage to property, Jacobs reached a deferred judgment agreement. He will have to meet a list of conditions for the next 12 months in order to have that charge dismissed by the state: no further criminal acts, no contact with the victim, supervision, counseling and restitution payment to the victim.

The presiding judge temporarily sealed the evidence from the case on Sept. 10 after Jacobs' no-contest plea.

On Tuesday, Sept. 15, attorneys representing Jacobs' ex-girlfriend, identified in court documents only as "ANM," filed a motion to permanently seal the evidence and discovery materials. If approved, the motion would prevent the NFL from reviewing surveillance camera footage of the incident as part of its investigation into Jacobs. NFL Media insider Ian Rapoport was the first to report that the league requested access to the video.

On Thursday, Sept. 17, the judge rejected the proposed order to seal the evidence, with online court records citing "improper format." The matter is "pending to be addressed" at a hearing set for Sept. 24.

Is Josh Jacobs getting suspended?

Jacobs has been on the commissioner's exempt list since Aug. 30. The exempt list is a form of administrative leave for players in specific circumstances related to criminal allegations, criminal felony or violence charges or possible violations of the NFL's personal conduct policy.

According to the collective bargaining agreement between the NFL and NFLPA, a standard suspension for a domestic violence case is six games. Suspensions can be longer depending on the severity of the case, which is part of why the league is trying to access video of the incident.

If Jacobs were to be suspended, any games he missed while on the commissioner's exempt list would count toward the suspension. The running back would also have to return the salary he earned while on the exempt list and remain unpaid throughout the period in which he's serving his suspension.

The NFL's likely eventual discipline for Jacobs is expected to be determined after his case is closed.

When will Josh Jacobs return to the Packers?

The timing of Jacobs' eventual return to the Packers will be determined by the length of the likely suspension the NFL will impose.

Based on the terms of the CBA, a six-game suspension is expected to be the minimum disciplinary action after Jacobs' plea included a misdemeanor battery conviction. That means the earliest possible return date for the running back would be in Week 7, when the Packers take on the Lions in Detroit on Oct. 25.

USA TODAY Sports' Nick Brinkerhoff contributed to this report.
